hand/geometric-langlands.html:
The Affine Grassmannian and the Geometric Satake Equivalence

The affine Grassmannian GrG = G(𝒦)/G(𝒪) — where 𝒦 = ℂ((t)) and 𝒪 = ℂ[[t]] — is an ind-scheme that parametrizes G-bundles on the formal disc with a trivialization on the punctured disc. Its geometry provides the local model for the Hecke correspondences used in the geometric Langlands program. The geometric Satake equivalence, proved by Ginzburg, Mirković–Vilonen, and others, establishes a tensor equivalence between the category of spherical perverse sheaves on GrG (with convolution product) and the category of finite-dimensional representations of the Langlands dual group LG. This equivalence is the local geometric counterpart of the classical Satake isomorphism for p-adic groups. The convolution product on perverse sheaves corresponds to the tensor product of representations, and the fiber functor is given by the global sections functor. The affine Grassmannian also carries a natural action of the loop group G(𝒦), and its Schubert varieties are indexed by dominant coweights of G, which correspond to dominant weights of LG. The geometric Satake equivalence is functorial with respect to homomorphisms of reductive groups and compatible with the nearby cycles functor, linking it to the monodromy of the Hitchin system. In the geometric Langlands correspondence, the Hecke operators at a point x ∈ X are defined by modifying a G-bundle at x using the affine Grassmannian; the geometric Satake equivalence identifies the eigenvalues of these Hecke operators with LG-local systems. This local-to-global principle is central: the global Hecke eigensheaf condition is built from the local geometric Satake data. The affine Grassmannian also appears in the construction of the Whittaker category and the geometric Casselman–Shalika formula, which expresses the Whittaker functions of automorphic forms in terms of the geometry of GrG. Recent work by Braverman–Finkelberg–Nakajima extends the geometric Satake to the Coulomb branches of 3d N=4 gauge theories, providing a physical interpretation via mirror symmetry.

The Categorical Geometric Langlands Conjecture and Ind-Coherent Sheaves

The categorical geometric Langlands conjecture, formulated by Gaitsgory and Lurie, asserts an equivalence of derived ∞-categories: D-mod(BunG) ≃ IndCohNilp(LocSysLG), where the right-hand side is the category of ind-coherent sheaves on the stack of LG-local systems with nilpotent singular support. This formulation replaces the earlier naive version using quasi-coherent sheaves on LocSysLG, which fails to capture the correct categorical structure because the stack of local systems is highly singular and non-smooth. Ind-coherent sheaves, introduced by Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum, behave like coherent sheaves on smooth schemes but are well-behaved on arbitrary derived stacks. The nilpotent singular support condition restricts to the global nilpotent cone, which is the image of the Hitchin fibration’s zero fiber under the non-Abelian Hodge correspondence. The equivalence is expected to be compatible with the natural monoidal structures: convolution of D-modules on BunG (coming from the Hecke correspondences) corresponds to the tensor product of ind-coherent sheaves on LocSysLG. The proof strategy uses the theory of chiral algebras and factorization algebras on the Ran space of the curve X. The chiral algebra of D-modules on BunG is identified with the chiral algebra of the affine Kac–Moody algebra at the critical level, which by the Feigin–Frenkel theorem is isomorphic to the algebra of functions on the space of LG-opers. This provides a bridge to the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence. The categorical equivalence also implies the classical geometric Langlands correspondence by taking the category of compact objects and passing to the Grothendieck group. The technology of derived algebraic geometry, in particular the theory of prestacks and the six-functor formalism for ind-coherent sheaves, is essential for the formulation and proof. Recent progress by Gaitsgory, Lurie, and others has established the conjecture for GLn and for tori, and has developed the necessary foundations for the general reductive case.

Worked Example: Hecke Eigensheaf Condition via Geometric Satake
Let G = SL2 and X = ℙ1. Describe how the geometric Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian GrSL2 identifies the eigenvalue of the Hecke operator at a point x ∈ X with a rank-2 local system on X.
The affine Grassmannian GrSL2 has Schubert varieties indexed by dominant coweights of SL2, i.e., non-negative integers n. The geometric Satake equivalence sends the intersection cohomology complex ICn of the Schubert variety Grn to the irreducible representation Vn of LG = PGL2 of dimension n+1. The Hecke operator Hx at x acts on a D-module ℱ on BunSL2 by the correspondence: BunSL2 ← Heckex → BunSL2 × X, where the fiber of Heckex over a bundle ℰ is GrSL2. The eigenvalue condition for ℱ to be a Hecke eigensheaf with eigenvalue a local system ℰ on X is that for each n, the action of Hx via ICn yields ℱ ⊠ Vn(ℰ), where Vn(ℰ) is the vector bundle associated to ℰ via the representation Vn. The geometric Satake equivalence guarantees that the convolution of ICn with ℱ corresponds to the tensor product of the corresponding representation of LG with the fiber of ℰ. Thus the eigenvalue local system ℰ is precisely the LG-local system whose monodromy gives the eigenvalues of the Hecke operators.
Exam Strategy: Categorical vs Classical Statements
When a question asks for the geometric Langlands correspondence, distinguish between the classical statement (equivalence of derived categories of D-modules and quasi-coherent sheaves) and the categorical statement (equivalence of D-mod(BunG) with IndCohNilp(LocSysLG)). The categorical version is the correct modern formulation; the classical version is a shadow obtained by taking compact objects. Examiners often test whether you know that quasi-coherent sheaves on LocSysLG are insufficient because LocSys is not smooth. Remember the nilpotent singular support condition and the role of ind-coherent sheaves.

The Quantum Geometric Langlands at Critical Level and the Feigin–Frenkel Center

The quantum geometric Langlands correspondence depends on a parameter ℏ = 1/(k + h∨), where k is the level of the affine Kac–Moody algebra and h∨ is the dual Coxeter number. The critical level corresponds to k = -h∨, i.e., ℏ → ∞. At this level, the center of the completed universal enveloping algebra of the affine Kac–Moody algebra, known as the Feigin–Frenkel center, becomes large and isomorphic to the algebra of functions on the space of LG-opers on the formal disc. An oper is a G-bundle with a connection and a reduction to a Borel subgroup satisfying a transversality condition; the space of LG-opers on X is a finite-dimensional variety that embeds into LocSysLG(X). The Feigin–Frenkel theorem states that the center of the affine vertex algebra at critical level is canonically isomorphic to the algebra of functions on the space of LG-opers on the formal disc. This provides a commutative algebra of quantum Hamiltonians for the quantum Hitchin system. In the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence, the category of k-twisted D-modules on BunG at critical level is expected to be equivalent to the category of modules over the sheaf of chiral differential operators on LocSysLG supported on the oper locus. The classical limit ℏ → 0 (i.e., k → ∞) recovers the classical geometric Langlands correspondence, where the quantum Hitchin Hamiltonians become the classical Hitchin Hamiltonians and the oper locus becomes the global nilpotent cone. The critical level is also where the KZ/WZW correspondence relates the quantum Hitchin connection to the monodromy of the Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations. The Bethe ansatz equations for the quantum Gaudin model, which is the quantum Hitchin system for G = SL2, are identified with the condition that a LG-oper has trivial monodromy. This links the quantum geometric Langlands to the theory of quantum integrable systems and the Langlands correspondence for the loop group.

Opers, Miura Transformations, and the Classical Limit

An oper for a reductive group G on a curve X is a triple (ℰ, ∇, ℰB) where ℰ is a G-bundle, ∇ is a connection, and ℰB is a reduction to a Borel subgroup B ⊂ G such that the induced map ℰB ×B (𝔤/𝔟) → ℰ ×G 𝔤 is an isomorphism. The space of G-opers, OpG(X), is a finite-dimensional affine space modeled on the Hitchin base B = ⊕i H0(X, Kdi+1), where di are the exponents of G. The Miura transformation is a map from the space of G-opers to the space of G-local systems with a full flag, given by forgetting the oper transversality condition. The image of the Miura transformation is the space of Miura opers, which are local systems with a flag preserved by the connection. The classical geometric Langlands correspondence relates D-modules on BunG to quasi-coherent sheaves on LocSysLG. In the classical limit of the quantum geometric Langlands, the category of k-twisted D-modules for large k localizes to the oper locus: the quantum Hamiltonians become the classical Hitchin Hamiltonians, and the eigenvalues of the quantum Hitchin system are given by opers. The Feigin–Frenkel center at critical level provides a quantization of the Hitchin Hamiltonians, and its spectrum is the space of LG-opers. The classical limit ℏ → 0 corresponds to the limit where the quantum parameter goes to zero, and the oper locus becomes the global nilpotent cone inside the Hitchin fiber. The Miura transformation then relates the oper locus to the space of local systems with a Borel reduction, which is the fiber of the map from the moduli of local systems with a flag to the Hitchin base. This geometry underlies the construction of Hecke eigensheaves via the Hitchin fibration: the spectral data of a Higgs bundle is a point in the Hitchin base, and the corresponding local system is obtained by solving the oper equations. The work of Beilinson–Drinfeld on the quantization of the Hitchin system and the construction of the quantum Hitchin connection uses the language of D-modules on the moduli stack of G-bundles and the chiral algebra of the affine Kac–Moody algebra.

The Geometric Langlands Correspondence for Parabolic Bundles and Ramification

The geometric Langlands correspondence extends to the setting of parabolic bundles and ramified local systems. A parabolic G-bundle on a curve X with marked points D = {x1, …, xn} is a G-bundle equipped with a reduction to a parabolic subgroup Pi ⊂ G at each xi and a weight in the dominant chamber of the Levi quotient. The moduli stack BunG(X, D) of parabolic bundles is a smooth algebraic stack. On the Galois side, one considers LG-local systems on X D with prescribed monodromy around the punctures, i.e., local systems with regular singularities and fixed conjugacy classes of monodromy. The geometric Langlands correspondence with ramification asserts an equivalence between the derived category of D-modules on BunG(X, D) (with appropriate twists) and the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves on the stack of LG-local systems with the prescribed ramification data. The Hecke operators are modified at the marked points: they allow modifications of the parabolic structure according to the representation theory of the Levi subgroups. The geometric Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian of the parabolic group (or the affine flag variety) provides the local eigenvalues. The Hitchin fibration for parabolic Higgs bundles has a base that includes the residues of the Higgs field at the marked points, and the fibers are again Abelian varieties (Prym varieties of spectral curves with marked points). The quantum geometric Langlands with ramification introduces a level k for each marked point, and the quantum Hitchin system becomes the quantum Gaudin model with inhomogeneities. The Bethe ansatz equations for the Gaudin model correspond to the condition that the oper has the prescribed monodromy. This ramified correspondence is essential for the geometric Langlands program over ℙ1 with three marked points, which is related to the quantum geometric Langlands for the quantum group at a root of unity and to the representation theory of the Virasoro algebra. The work of Frenkel–Gross and others connects the ramified geometric Langlands to the theory of rigid local systems and the geometric Langlands correspondence for the loop group.

  • Common Trap: Confusing the affine Grassmannian with the affine flag variety; the former gives the spherical Hecke category, the latter gives the Iwahori-Hecke category.
  • Common Trap: Assuming the classical geometric Langlands uses quasi-coherent sheaves on the whole LocSys; the correct target is ind-coherent sheaves with nilpotent singular support.
  • Common Trap: Forgetting that the critical level is k = -h∨, not k = 0; the parameter ℏ = 1/(k + h∨) diverges at critical level.
  • Common Trap: Mixing up the Miura transformation (oper → local system with flag) with the non-Abelian Hodge correspondence (Higgs bundle → local system).
  • Common Trap: Thinking the quantum geometric Langlands is only a deformation of the classical one; at critical level it is a completely different categorical equivalence involving chiral algebras.
  • Common Trap: Overlooking the role of the Feigin–Frenkel center as the algebra of quantum Hitchin Hamiltonians; it is the center of the affine vertex algebra at critical level.
  • Common Trap: Neglecting that parabolic structures require modifications of both the automorphic and Galois sides, and that the Hecke operators at marked points involve the affine flag variety of the Levi subgroup.

hand/geometry.html:
Coordinate Geometry – Distance, Section Formula, and Locus

Coordinate geometry translates geometric problems into algebraic equations, allowing the use of algebraic manipulation to solve for lengths, mid‑points, and loci. The distance between two points P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) in the Cartesian plane is derived from the Pythagorean theorem: PQ = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²]. This formula extends to three dimensions as √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²]. The section formula gives the coordinates of a point dividing a line segment internally in the ratio m:n as ((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n), (my₂+ny₁)/(m+n)); for external division the signs of m and n are opposite. The midpoint is the special case m=n, yielding ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a given geometric condition. For example, the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB. The locus of points at a constant distance r from a fixed point O is a circle with equation (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r² where O(h,k). The locus of points where the sum of distances to two fixed points (foci) is constant is an ellipse; the difference of distances constant gives a hyperbola. These definitions lead directly to the standard equations of conics.

The slope of a line through P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂) is m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁). Two lines are parallel iff their slopes are equal; they are perpendicular iff the product of their slopes is −1 (provided neither is vertical). The equation of a line in slope‑intercept form is y = mx + c; in point‑slope form y−y₁ = m(x−x₁); and in intercept form x/a + y/b = 1. The general form Ax + By + C = 0 is useful for finding the distance from a point (x₀,y₀) to the line: |Ax₀+By₀+C|/√(A²+B²).

Applications include finding the area of a triangle given vertices (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃) via the determinant formula Area = ½|x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)|. The condition for collinearity of three points is that this area equals zero. The centroid of a triangle with vertices (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃) is ((x₁+x₂+x₃)/3, (y₁+y₂+y₃)/3). The circumcenter and orthocenter can also be located by solving perpendicular bisector and altitude equations respectively.

Examiners often combine coordinate geometry with other topics: a circle may be defined by three points, requiring the solution of a system of three equations to find its centre and radius; a triangle’s area may be asked after a transformation such as a rotation of axes. Mastery of algebraic manipulation, especially completing the square to convert general second‑degree equations into standard forms, is essential for speed.

Conic Sections – Parabola, Ellipse, Hyperbola

Conic sections arise from intersecting a plane with a double‑napped right circular cone. The angle of the plane relative to the cone’s axis determines the curve: a plane parallel to a generator yields a parabola; a plane cutting both nappes yields a hyperbola; a plane cutting one nappe at an angle less than the generator yields an ellipse; a plane perpendicular to the axis yields a circle (a special ellipse). Each conic can be defined by a focus‑directrix property: the set of points where the distance to a fixed point (focus) equals e times the distance to a fixed line (directrix). The eccentricity e characterises the conic: e = 1 for parabola, 0 < e < 1 for ellipse, e > 1 for hyperbola, and e = 0 for circle.

The standard equation of a parabola with vertex at the origin and axis along the x‑axis is y² = 4ax (focus (a,0), directrix x = −a). If the axis is along the y‑axis the equation is x² = 4ay. The latus rectum length is |4a|. For an ellipse centred at the origin with major axis along the x‑axis: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 where a > b. The foci are at (±c,0) with c² = a²−b². Eccentricity e = c/a. The latus rectum length is 2b²/a. For a hyperbola centred at the origin with transverse axis along the x‑axis: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. Foci at (±c,0) with c² = a²+b². Eccentricity e = c/a > 1. The asymptotes are the lines y = ±(b/a)x.

Parametric representations simplify many problems: parabola (at², 2at), ellipse (a cosθ, b sinθ), hyperbola (a secθ, b tanθ) or (a cosh t, b sinh t). The equation of the tangent to a conic at a point (x₁,y₁) on it can be written by replacing x² → xx₁, y² → yy₁, x → (x+x₁)/2, y → (y+y₁)/2 in the standard equation (the “T = 0” method). The chord of contact from an external point (x₀,y₀) is obtained similarly. The director circle of an ellipse is x²+y² = a²+b²; for a hyperbola it is x²+y² = a²−b² (real only if a > b).

Important properties: the reflection property of a parabola – rays parallel to the axis reflect through the focus; for an ellipse, rays from one focus reflect to the other focus; for a hyperbola, rays directed toward one focus reflect as if coming from the other focus. These properties underlie applications in optics and satellite dish design. The polar equation of a conic with one focus at the pole is r = ed/(1+e cosθ) where d is the distance from the focus to the directrix.

Examiners frequently ask for the locus of the midpoint of a chord of a conic that passes through a fixed point, or the equation of a common tangent to two conics. Solving these requires eliminating parameters or using the condition that a line y = mx + c touches a conic (discriminant zero). For a parabola y² = 4ax, the condition of tangency is c = a/m. For an ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, the condition is c² = a²m² + b². For a hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, the condition is c² = a²m² − b².

Worked Example – Common Tangent to Parabola and Ellipse
Find the equation of a line that is tangent to both the parabola y² = 8x and the ellipse x²/9 + y²/4 = 1.
For the parabola y² = 8x, we have 4a = 8 ⇒ a = 2. A tangent in slope form is y = mx + a/m = mx + 2/m. For the ellipse x²/9 + y²/4 = 1, the tangency condition for y = mx + c is c² = a²m² + b² = 9m² + 4. Substitute c = 2/m: (2/m)² = 9m² + 4 ⇒ 4/m² = 9m² + 4. Multiply by m²: 4 = 9m⁴ + 4m² ⇒ 9m⁴ + 4m² − 4 = 0. Let u = m² ≥ 0: 9u² + 4u − 4 = 0. Solve: u = [−4 ± √(16 + 144)]/(18) = [−4 ± √160]/18 = [−4 ± 4√10]/18 = [−2 ± 2√10]/9. Only the positive root is valid: u = (−2 + 2√10)/9 = 2(√10−1)/9. Thus m = ±√u. The corresponding c = 2/m. Hence there are two common tangents symmetric about the x‑axis. Their equations are y = mx + 2/m with m = ±√[2(√10−1)/9].
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the tangency conditions for the three standard conics in slope form; they turn a locus or common‑tangent problem into a simple algebraic equation in m. When a problem gives a point and asks for the chord of contact, write the “T = 0” equation directly instead of finding the two tangents separately. For ellipse and hyperbola, keep the director‑circle equations handy to test whether a given point lies outside the conic (real tangents exist only if the point satisfies the director‑circle inequality).

Advanced Circle Theorems – Power of a Point and Radical Axis

The power of a point P with respect to a circle of radius r and centre O is defined as Pow(P) = OP² − r². If P lies outside the circle, the power equals the square of the length of the tangent from P to the circle; if P lies inside, the power is negative and its absolute value equals the product of the segments of any chord through P. For a secant through P intersecting the circle at A and B, PA × PB = |Pow(P)|. This theorem unifies tangent‑secant and intersecting‑chord results.

The radical axis of two circles is the locus of points having equal power with respect to both circles. Given circles C₁: x²+y²+2g₁x+2f₁y+c₁=0 and C₂: x²+y²+2g₂x+2f₂y+c₂=0, subtracting the equations eliminates the quadratic terms and yields the linear equation of the radical axis: 2(g₁−g₂)x + 2(f₁−f₂)y + (c₁−c₂) = 0. This line is perpendicular to the line joining the centres. If the circles intersect, the radical axis is the common chord; if they touch, it is the common tangent at the point of contact; if they are separate, it lies between them.

The radical centre of three circles (taken in pairs) is the unique point where the three radical axes concur, provided the centres are not collinear. This point has equal power with respect to all three circles. It is the centre of the unique circle orthogonal to all three given circles. Orthogonal circles satisfy 2g₁g₂ + 2f₁f₂ = c₁ + c₂ (derived from the condition that the radius of one circle drawn to the intersection point is tangent to the other).

Coaxial systems are families of circles sharing the same radical axis. The limiting points of a coaxial system are the two points (real or imaginary) that have zero power with respect to every circle in the system; they are the point circles of the family. Any circle orthogonal to two circles of a coaxial system is orthogonal to the whole system. These concepts appear in problems asking for the equation of a circle cutting three given circles orthogonally, or for the locus of centres of circles touching two given circles.

Applications: Given two intersecting circles, the length of the common chord can be found using the distance between centres d and radii r₁, r₂: chord length = 2√[r₁² − ((r₁²−r₂²+d²)/(2d))²]. The radical axis also provides a quick way to find the equation of a circle passing through the intersection points of two given circles: C₁ + λC₂ = 0 (where C₁=0 and C₂=0 are the circle equations) represents the family of circles through their intersections; the radical axis corresponds to λ = −1.

Solid Geometry – Frustum, Prism, Pyramid, and Composite Solids

A frustum is the portion of a cone or pyramid that remains after the top is cut off by a plane parallel to the base. For a conical frustum with radii R (lower base) and r (upper base) and height h, the slant height l = √[(R−r)² + h²]. Volume V = (πh/3)(R² + Rr + r²). Curved surface area CSA = π(R+r)l. Total surface area adds the areas of the two circular bases: TSA = π(R+r)l + πR² + πr². For a pyramidal frustum with base areas A₁ and A₂ and height h, volume V = (h/3)(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)). The lateral surface area is the sum of the areas of the trapezoidal faces.

A prism is a polyhedron with two congruent parallel polygonal bases and rectangular lateral faces. For a right prism, the lateral edges are perpendicular to the bases. Volume V = Base Area × Height. Lateral surface area LSA = Perimeter of Base × Height. Total surface area TSA = LSA + 2 × Base Area. A right circular cylinder is a prism with a circular base; its formulas match the cylinder formulas already known.

A pyramid has a polygonal base and triangular faces meeting at a common vertex. For a right pyramid (vertex projected onto the centroid of the base), the slant height of each triangular face can be found using the apothem of the base and the pyramid height. Volume V = (1/3) × Base Area × Height. Lateral surface area is the sum of the areas of the triangular faces; for a regular pyramid with base perimeter P and slant height l, LSA = ½Pl. The total surface area adds the base area.

Composite solids are formed by combining or removing basic solids. Typical exam problems: a cylinder with a conical cavity drilled through its axis; a hemisphere mounted on a cylinder; a cube with a hemispherical depression on each face. The key principle is that volumes add or subtract, while surface areas require careful accounting of which faces become internal and are no longer exposed. For example, when a cone is removed from a cylinder sharing the same base and height, the remaining volume is V_cyl − V_cone = πr²h − (1/3)πr²h = (2/3)πr²h. The new total surface area is the cylinder’s curved surface plus the cone’s curved surface plus the base of the cylinder (the top base is removed).

Another common scenario: a solid sphere of radius R is melted and recast into a number of identical smaller spheres or into a wire (cylinder). Volume conservation gives n × (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)πR³ ⇒ r = R/∛n. For a wire of length L and radius r, πr²L = (4/3)πR³ ⇒ r = √[(4R³)/(3L)]. These problems test algebraic manipulation and unit consistency.

Transformation Geometry – Reflection, Rotation, Translation, and Scaling

Transformation geometry studies how figures move in the plane or space while preserving certain properties. An isometry (rigid motion) preserves distances and angles; the four basic plane isometries are translation, rotation, reflection, and glide reflection. A translation by vector v = (a,b) maps (x,y) → (x+a, y+b). A rotation about the origin by angle θ (counter‑clockwise) maps (x,y) → (x cosθ − y sinθ, x sinθ + y cosθ). A reflection across the x‑axis maps (x,y) → (x,−y); across the y‑axis (−x,y); across the line y = x maps (x,y) → (y,x); across y = −x maps (−y,−x). A glide reflection is a reflection followed by a translation parallel to the mirror line.

These transformations can be represented by 2×2 matrices (for linear part) plus a translation vector. Rotation matrix: [[cosθ, −sinθ],[sinθ, cosθ]]. Reflection across a line through the origin with unit direction vector u = (cosα, sinα) has matrix [[cos2α, sin2α],[sin2α, −cos2α]]. Composition of transformations corresponds to matrix multiplication (for the linear parts) and vector addition for translations. The determinant of the linear part is +1 for rotations and translations (orientation‑preserving) and −1 for reflections and glide reflections (orientation‑reversing).

Scaling (dilation) about the origin by factor k maps (x,y) → (kx, ky). It is not an isometry unless |k| = 1. A similarity transformation is a composition of an isometry and a scaling; it preserves angles and ratios of lengths. The matrix of a similarity is k × R where R is an orthogonal matrix (rotation or reflection). In coordinate geometry, a homothety with centre C(x₀,y₀) and ratio k maps P(x,y) → (x₀ + k(x−x₀), y₀ + k(y−y₀)).

Invariants under isometries: distances, angles, area, orientation (for proper isometries). Under similarities: angles, ratios of lengths, ratio of areas = k². Under affine transformations (which include shear), parallelism and ratios of segments on parallel lines are preserved, but angles and lengths are not. Exam questions often ask: “Triangle ABC is reflected in the line y = 2x + 1 and then rotated 90° about the origin. Find the coordinates of the image of vertex A.” The efficient method is to apply the transformation matrices sequentially or to find the single equivalent transformation matrix.

In three dimensions, the basic isometries are translation, rotation about an axis, reflection in a plane, and rotatory reflection (improper rotation). A rotation about the z‑axis by angle θ has matrix [[cosθ, −sinθ, 0],[sinθ, cosθ, 0],[0,0,1]]. Reflection in the xy‑plane is diag(1,1,−1). The composition of two reflections in intersecting planes is a rotation about their line of intersection by twice the angle between the planes. These facts are useful for solving problems involving symmetry of polyhedra or for finding the image of a point after multiple reflections.

  • Confusing the power of a point formula with the tangent length formula; remember power = OP² − r², tangent² = power only when P is outside.
  • Forgetting that the radical axis is a line, not a segment; it extends infinitely even if the circles do not intersect.
  • Using the frustum volume formula for a truncated pyramid without adjusting for base shapes; the pyramidal frustum uses base areas, not radii.
  • Neglecting to subtract the area of the base that becomes internal when two solids are joined; total surface area is not simply the sum of individual surface areas.
  • Applying 2D rotation matrices to 3D problems without adding the third coordinate; always embed the 2D matrix in a 3×3 identity block for the unchanged axis.
  • Assuming a similarity transformation preserves area; area scales by k², not by k.
  • Master these pitfalls to avoid losing marks on geometry questions.

hand/cobordism-theory.html:
Unoriented Cobordism and the Thom Spectrum MO

The unoriented cobordism ring Ω*O was the first cobordism ring to be completely computed. Thom proved in 1954 that the Pontryagin–Thom construction yields an isomorphism ΩnO ≅ πn(MO), where MO is the Thom spectrum of the universal real vector bundle over BO. The homotopy groups of MO are known to be a polynomial algebra over the field 𝔽2 on one generator in each dimension that is not a power of two. Concretely,

Ω*O ≅ 𝔽2[xi | i ≠ 2k], |xi| = i.

The generators can be represented by the real projective spaces ℝℙi for i not a power of two. The Stiefel–Whitney numbers give a complete set of invariants: two closed smooth manifolds are unoriented cobordant if and only if all their Stiefel–Whitney numbers agree. This result makes unoriented cobordism a purely algebraic theory over 𝔽2 and provides the foundation for the Adams spectral sequence based on MO.

Key computational tools

  • The Thom isomorphism H*(MO; 𝔽2) ≅ H*(BO; 𝔽2) identifies the cohomology of MO with the polynomial algebra 𝔽2[w1, w2, …] on the universal Stiefel–Whitney classes.
  • The Steenrod algebra action on H*(MO) is determined by the Wu formula, allowing the Adams spectral sequence to collapse at the E2-page and yield the polynomial description above.
  • The Conner–Floyd theorem for MO states that MO*(X) ⊗MO* 𝔽2 ≅ H*(X; 𝔽2), showing that unoriented cobordism is the universal 𝔽2-oriented cohomology theory.

Oriented Cobordism and the Thom Spectrum MSO

Oriented cobordism Ω*SO is richer because the coefficient ring contains torsion. Thom’s Pontryagin–Thom construction gives ΩnSO ≅ πn(MSO), where MSO is the Thom spectrum of the universal oriented bundle over BSO. Rationally, the ring is a polynomial algebra on the even‑dimensional complex projective spaces:

Ω*SO ⊗ ℚ ≅ ℚ[ℂℙ2, ℂℙ4, ℂℙ6, …].

Integrally, the structure was determined by Wall (1960) and later refined by Milnor and Stong. The ring Ω*SO is a polynomial algebra over ℤ on generators in dimensions 4k, together with ℤ/2‑torsion in dimensions 8k+1 and 8k+2. The Pontryagin numbers and the Stiefel–Whitney numbers (mod 2) together form a complete set of invariants for oriented cobordism. In particular, a closed oriented manifold bounds an oriented manifold if and only if all its Pontryagin numbers and all its Stiefel–Whitney numbers vanish.

Generators and relations

  • For each k ≥ 1 there is a generator y4k which can be taken as the Milnor hypersurface H2k,2k ⊂ ℂℙ2k × ℂℙ2k.
  • The 2‑torsion generators are detected by the Kervaire invariant and the Arf invariant of the associated quadratic forms on middle‑dimensional homology.
  • The Hirzebruch signature theorem expresses the signature of a 4k‑manifold as a polynomial in Pontryagin numbers; this polynomial is the L‑genus and gives the image of the signature homomorphism Ω4kSO → ℤ.
Worked example: computing an oriented cobordism class
Determine whether the product manifold ℂℙ2 × ℂℙ2 is zero in Ω8SO.
The oriented cobordism group Ω8SO is free abelian of rank two, generated by ℂℙ4 and ℂℙ2 × ℂℙ2. The Pontryagin numbers of ℂℙ2 × ℂℙ2 are p12 = 4 and p2 = 0, while for ℂℙ4 they are p12 = 25 and p2 = 10. Since the Pontryagin numbers of ℂℙ2 × ℂℙ2 are not all zero, the manifold is not null‑cobordant. Hence its class in Ω8SO is non‑zero.
Exam strategy
When a question asks for the cobordism class of a product, compute the Pontryagin numbers using the Whitney sum formula for tangent bundles. Compare the resulting numbers with the known basis of Ω*SO ⊗ ℚ; if they are linearly independent from the basis elements, the class is non‑zero. Memorise the first few Pontryagin numbers of ℂℙ2k and of the Milnor hypersurfaces to speed up calculations.

Spin Cobordism and the Anderson–Brown–Peterson Spectral Sequence

Spin cobordism Ω*Spin classifies manifolds equipped with a spin structure, i.e. a lift of the structure group from SO to Spin. The Pontryagin–Thom isomorphism identifies ΩnSpin with πn(MSpin), the homotopy groups of the Thom spectrum of the universal spin bundle over BSpin. Anderson, Brown, and Peterson (1966) constructed a spectral sequence

E2s,t = ExtA(1)s,t(H*(MSpin; 𝔽2), 𝔽2) ⇒ πt−s(MSpin)̂2,

where A(1) is the subalgebra of the Steenrod algebra generated by Sq1 and Sq2. This spectral sequence computes the 2‑completed spin cobordism groups and reveals the close relationship between MSpin and the real K‑theory spectrum KO. In low dimensions the groups are:

  • Ω0Spin ≅ ℤ, generated by a point.
  • Ω1Spin = Ω2Spin = 0.
  • Ω3Spin = 0.
  • Ω4Spin ≅ ℤ, generated by the K3 surface (signature −16).
  • Ω5Spin = Ω6Spin = 0.
  • Ω7Spin = 0.
  • Ω8Spin ≅ ℤ ⊕ ℤ, generated by the K3 surface squared and the Bott manifold.

The Â‑genus gives a ring homomorphism Ω*Spin → ℤ which is an isomorphism after tensoring with ℚ. The Anderson–Brown–Peterson spectral sequence also shows that the 2‑primary torsion in spin cobordism is detected by the KO‑theory orientation MSpin → KO.

Stratified Cobordism and Manifolds with Singularities

Classical cobordism theory assumes smooth closed manifolds. In many geometric problems one encounters spaces with singularities, such as algebraic varieties or orbit spaces of group actions. Stratified cobordism, developed by Quinn (1988) and extended by Siegel and others, provides a framework where the objects are stratified spaces (e.g. Whitney stratified sets) and the cobordisms are stratified maps satisfying transversality conditions on each stratum. The resulting cobordism groups Ω*strat fit into a long exact sequence relating them to the ordinary cobordism groups of the links of the strata.

Key features include:

  • The Thom–Mather isotopy theorem ensures that a stratified cobordism can be decomposed into elementary cobordisms along each stratum.
  • For a cone on a manifold L, the stratified cobordism class is determined by the ordinary cobordism class of L together with a choice of normal data.
  • The intersection homology groups of Goresky–MacPherson provide invariants of stratified spaces that are compatible with stratified cobordism; in particular, the signature of a Witt space is a stratified cobordism invariant.
  • Applications include the classification of singular algebraic varieties up to cobordism and the study of the topology of moduli spaces with boundary strata.

Surgery Theory and the Classification of High‑Dimensional Manifolds

Surgery theory, created by Browder, Novikov, Sullivan, and Wall in the 1960s, uses cobordism as a tool to classify manifolds up to diffeomorphism or homeomorphism in dimensions ≥ 5. The central object is the surgery exact sequence

⋯ → Ln+1(π1X) → 𝒮(X) → [X, G/O] → Ln(π1X) → ⋯

where 𝒮(X) is the structure set of manifolds homotopy equivalent to a given Poincaré complex X, [X, G/O] is the set of normal invariants (a cobordism group of degree‑one normal maps), and L*(π1X) are the Wall surgery obstruction groups. The map [X, G/O] → Ln(π1X) is the surgery obstruction; its kernel consists of normal invariants that can be realized by a homotopy equivalence.

Important consequences:

  • The s‑cobordism theorem: an h‑cobordism between simply‑connected manifolds of dimension ≥ 5 is trivial if and only if its Whitehead torsion vanishes.
  • The classification of exotic spheres: the group Θn of homotopy n‑spheres up to h‑cobordism fits into an exact sequence involving the stable homotopy groups of spheres and the image of the J‑homomorphism.
  • For simply‑connected manifolds, the surgery obstruction groups Ln(ℤ) are 8‑periodic: L4k ≅ ℤ (signature), L4k+2 ≅ ℤ/2 (Arf invariant), and the odd groups vanish.
  • The Novikov conjecture on homotopy invariance of higher signatures is equivalent to the injectivity of the assembly map in the surgery exact sequence for the group C*‑algebra.
  • Confusing unoriented and oriented cobordism invariants; Stiefel–Whitney numbers alone do not detect oriented cobordism.
  • Assuming the Pontryagin numbers generate all torsion in Ω*SO; 2‑torsion requires Stiefel–Whitney numbers as well.
  • Overlooking the role of the Anderson–Brown–Peterson spectral sequence in computing spin cobordism; it is not merely the Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence.
  • Treating stratified cobordism as ordinary cobordism of the underlying space; the link data and normal structures are essential.
  • Misapplying the surgery exact sequence to low‑dimensional manifolds (n ≤ 4) where the theory fails without additional hypotheses.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the structure set 𝒮(X) and the set of normal invariants [X, G/O]; they are related but not identical.
  • Forgetting that the Â‑genus vanishes on manifolds admitting positive scalar curvature, a key obstruction in spin geometry.

Mastering these advanced topics equips you to tackle the deepest problems in manifold topology and stable homotopy theory.

hand/math-epidemiology.html:
Age-Structured Compartmental Models and Contact Matrices

Age structure is introduced by replicating the SIR or SEIR compartments for each age group, typically 5‑year or 10‑year bands. The force of infection for age group i becomes λ_i = Σ_j β_ij I_j / N_j, where β_ij = q · c_ij captures the per‑contact transmission probability q multiplied by the average number of contacts that a person in group i has with persons in group j per unit time. The matrix C = (c_ij) is the contact matrix, often derived from diary‑based surveys such as POLYMOD or from mobile‑phone proximity data. The next‑generation matrix for the age‑structured system is K = (β_ij / γ) · diag(S_i0 / N_i), where S_i0 are the initial susceptibles. The basic reproduction number R₀ is the spectral radius (dominant eigenvalue) of K. This formulation shows that R₀ depends on both the contact pattern and the age distribution of susceptibility. Vaccination prioritisation can be analysed by reducing S_i0 in selected rows of K and recomputing the spectral radius; the optimal allocation often targets the age groups that contribute most to the dominant eigenvector of K. In practice, age‑structured models are essential for diseases with strong age‑dependent severity (e.g., COVID‑19, influenza) and for evaluating school‑closure policies, because the contact matrix changes dramatically when school contacts are removed.

Parameterising the contact matrix requires careful handling of reciprocity (c_ij N_i = c_ji N_j) and of missing data for older ages. Synthetic matrices can be generated by fitting a parametric form (e.g., a Gaussian kernel on age difference) to survey data. Sensitivity analysis typically varies the overall scaling factor q and the assortativeness of C to assess robustness of R₀ and of projected epidemic peaks. The final‑size relation for age‑structured models generalises the scalar equation to a system: 1 − s_i = exp(− Σ_j R₀_ij (1 − s_j)), where s_i = S_i(∞)/N_i. This system can be solved numerically and provides the expected attack rate in each age group.

Time-Varying Reproduction Number Estimation and Inference

The effective reproduction number R_t quantifies the average number of secondary cases generated by an infected individual at calendar time t, accounting for depletion of susceptibles and interventions. A widely used estimator (Cori et al., 2013) assumes that the incidence i(t) follows a Poisson process with mean R_t Σ_s i(t−s) w(s), where w(s) is the discretised serial‑interval distribution. Given a time series of daily incidence and a known w(s), the likelihood for R_t over a sliding window of length τ is L(R_t) = ∏t Poisson(i(t) | R_t Λ(t)), with Λ(t) = Σs=1τ i(t−s) w(s). A Gamma prior on R_t yields a conjugate Gamma posterior, enabling analytic computation of the posterior mean and credible intervals. The window length τ trades bias against variance: short windows track rapid changes but increase uncertainty; long windows smooth noise but lag behind true shifts. Alternative methods include the Wallinga‑Teunis approach, which attributes each case to a probable infector using the serial interval, and the EpiEstim package that implements the Cori method with Bayesian smoothing. All methods require a reliable serial‑interval distribution; misspecification of the mean or dispersion of w(s) biases R_t systematically. In practice, analysts report both the posterior median and the 95% credible interval, and they perform sensitivity checks by varying the serial‑interval parameters.

Estimating R_t with a Sliding‑Window Cori Method
Given daily incidence counts for 30 days and a discrete serial‑interval distribution w = (0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2) for lags 1–4 days, outline the steps to compute a 7‑day moving‑average estimate of R_t using the Cori et al. (2013) Bayesian framework with a Gamma(α=1, β=1) prior.
1. For each day t = 8 … 30, compute the total infectiousness Λ(t) = Σs=14 i(t−s) w(s). 2. The likelihood for R_t over the window is Poisson(i(t) | R_t Λ(t)). 3. With a Gamma(α, β) prior, the posterior is Gamma(α + Σt i(t), β + Σt Λ(t)). 4. The posterior mean is (α + Σ i) / (β + Σ Λ); the 95% credible interval uses the Gamma quantiles. 5. Repeat for each window, shifting by one day, to obtain a time series of R_t estimates.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to distinguish R₀ from R_t, state that R₀ is a fixed threshold for a wholly susceptible population, while R_t is a time‑dependent quantity reflecting current susceptibility, interventions, and behavioural change. Mention that R_t can be estimated from incidence data using the serial interval, whereas R₀ requires the next‑generation matrix at the disease‑free equilibrium.

Multi-Strain Competition and Variant Dynamics

Multi‑strain models extend the compartmental framework by indexing each strain k with its own infected compartments I_k and, if needed, strain‑specific susceptibility. Cross‑immunity is introduced through a matrix σkl that reduces susceptibility to strain l after recovery from strain k; σkk=1 (full immunity to the same strain) and 0 ≤ σkl ≤ 1 for k ≠ l. The force of infection for strain l becomes λ_l = Σ_k β_l I_k / N, where β_l may differ across strains due to transmissibility changes. The next‑generation matrix becomes block‑structured, and the invasion reproduction number for strain l in a population where strain k is endemic is Rl|k = (β_l / γ_l) · (S_k^* / N) · (1 − σkl), where S_k^* is the susceptible fraction at the single‑strain equilibrium. Competitive exclusion occurs when the strain with the highest R₀ outcompetes all others, but stable coexistence is possible if cross‑immunity is asymmetric or if strains occupy distinct ecological niches (e.g., age groups). Variant replacement dynamics, as observed with SARS‑CoV‑2, are modelled by allowing β_l to increase over time (e.g., due to mutations) and by incorporating waning immunity. The effective reproduction number of a new variant in a partially immune population is R_eff = R₀_variant × (1 − p_immune × σ), where p_immune is the proportion immune to the ancestral strain and σ is the cross‑protection factor. Phylodynamic inference couples the epidemiological model with a coalescent process to estimate transmission rates from genetic sequences, providing a joint estimate of R_t and the rate of adaptive evolution.

Optimal Control with Resource Constraints and Cost‑Effectiveness

Optimal control theory formulates vaccination or non‑pharmaceutical interventions as time‑dependent control functions u(t) that minimise a cost functional J = ∫₀^T [A I(t) + B u(t)²] dt subject to the state equations (e.g., SIR with vaccination). The Hamiltonian H = A I + B u² + λ_S (−β S I / N − u S) + λ_I (β S I / N − γ I) + λ_R (γ I + u S) yields adjoint equations dλ/dt = −∂H/∂state with transversality conditions λ(T)=0. Pontryagin's maximum principle gives the optimal control u*(t) = max(0, min(u_max, (λ_S − λ_R) S / (2B))). When vaccine supply is limited, an integral constraint ∫₀^T u(t) dt ≤ V_total is added, leading to a Lagrange multiplier that modifies the switching function. Cost‑effectiveness analysis compares the incremental cost‑effectiveness ratio (ICER) = (Cost_intervention − Cost_baseline) / (QALYs_gained) against a willingness‑to‑pay threshold. In age‑structured models, the control becomes a vector u_i(t) for each age group, and the Hamiltonian includes a sum over i. The optimal allocation often follows a “priority‑by‑eigenvector” rule: vaccinate groups with the largest components of the dominant left eigenvector of the next‑generation matrix, because they contribute most to transmission. Numerical solution uses forward‑backward sweep methods or direct transcription with nonlinear programming solvers. Sensitivity of the optimal policy to parameter uncertainty is assessed by sampling from the joint distribution of β, γ, and cost parameters and re‑optimising.

Data Assimilation, Forecasting, and Model Uncertainty

Data assimilation merges noisy surveillance data (case counts, hospitalisations, seroprevalence) with the dynamical model to produce calibrated state estimates and short‑term forecasts. Sequential Monte Carlo (particle filter) methods propagate an ensemble of model states, weight them by the likelihood of observed data, and resample to avoid degeneracy. The ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) approximates the forecast distribution as Gaussian and updates the mean and covariance using the Kalman gain; it is computationally efficient for high‑dimensional age‑structured models. Bayesian melding combines prior distributions on parameters with a likelihood based on the discrepancy between model output and data, yielding posterior parameter distributions via Markov chain Monte Carlo. Forecast skill is evaluated using proper scoring rules such as the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) or the logarithmic score. Structural uncertainty — the choice between SIR, SEIR, or network models — is addressed by multi‑model ensembles, where each model receives a weight proportional to its predictive performance (e.g., stacking). Global sensitivity analysis (Sobol indices) quantifies the contribution of each parameter (β, γ, contact matrix entries) to output variance (peak incidence, final size). Scenario analysis explores counterfactual intervention timelines (e.g., earlier lockdown, higher vaccine coverage) by re‑simulating the calibrated model with modified control functions. Transparent reporting of prediction intervals, model assumptions, and data limitations is essential for policy relevance.

  • Confusing R₀ with R_t: R₀ is a fixed threshold at the disease‑free equilibrium; R_t varies with susceptibility and interventions.
  • Assuming the serial interval equals the generation interval; they differ when pre‑symptomatic transmission occurs.
  • Neglecting reciprocity in contact matrices, leading to non‑physical asymmetric mixing.
  • Treating cross‑immunity as symmetric when empirical data often show asymmetric protection between strains.
  • Ignoring the integral vaccine‑supply constraint in optimal control, producing infeasible vaccination schedules.
  • Using a single deterministic forecast without quantifying parameter or structural uncertainty.
  • Overlooking the need for proper scoring rules to compare forecast models objectively.

hand/heegaard-floer.html:
The Ozsváth–Szabó Spectral Sequence from Khovanov Homology to Heegaard Floer Homology

Ozsváth and Szabó constructed a spectral sequence whose E²‑page is the reduced Khovanov homology Kh(K) of a knot K ⊂ S³ and which converges to the hat version of knot Floer homology HFK̂(K). The construction uses a cube of resolutions of a knot diagram, each vertex equipped with a Heegaard diagram for the corresponding resolution. The differential on the E¹‑page counts holomorphic disks in the symmetric product that correspond to the Khovanov differential; higher differentials arise from disks with more complicated domain multiplicities. The spectral sequence is functorial under knot cobordisms and respects the Alexander grading, so the Alexander polynomial appears as the Euler characteristic of both the E²‑page and the limit. A key consequence is that the rank of HFK̂(K) is bounded above by the rank of Kh(K), giving a new proof that the knot Floer homology of an alternating knot is determined by its Alexander polynomial. The spectral sequence also implies that the Rasmussen invariant s(K) (defined from Khovanov homology) and the Ozsváth–Szabó τ‑invariant (defined from knot Floer homology) satisfy s(K) = 2τ(K) for quasi‑alternating knots, a fact that has been used to compute slice genera of many knots.

Bordered Heegaard Floer Homology and the Pairing Theorem

Bordered Heegaard Floer homology, developed by Lipshitz, Ozsváth, and Thurston, assigns to a 3‑manifold with parametrized boundary a differential graded module over the algebra A(F) associated to the boundary surface F. For a surface of genus g with one boundary component, A(F) is generated by Reeb chords on a pointed matched circle; its differential encodes the combinatorics of holomorphic curves in the symmetric product of F. A bordered Heegaard diagram consists of a Heegaard surface with α‑ and β‑curves together with a set of arcs representing the boundary parametrization. The resulting module CFD(Y) (type D) or CFA(Y) (type A) is computed by counting holomorphic disks with boundary on the α‑ and β‑curves and with asymptotics given by Reeb chords. The pairing theorem states that if Y = Y₁ ∪F Y₂ is a decomposition along a surface F, then the closed‑manifold invariant CF̂(Y) is homotopy equivalent to the derived tensor product CFA(Y₁) ⊠ CFD(Y₂). This theorem reduces the computation of Heegaard Floer homology for arbitrary 3‑manifolds to the computation of bordered modules for elementary pieces (handlebodies, solid tori, and mapping cylinders). In practice, one builds a library of bordered modules for standard building blocks and then uses the pairing theorem together with a computer implementation of the algebra A(F) to obtain HF̂ for large families of manifolds, including all manifolds obtained by Dehn surgery on knots in S³ up to a given crossing number.

Worked Example: Computing HF̂ of a Lens Space via the Pairing Theorem
Let L(p,q) be the lens space obtained by p/q‑surgery on the unknot. Decompose L(p,q) as the union of a solid torus V (the surgery solid torus) and the complement of the unknot, which is also a solid torus U. Both pieces have torus boundary. Compute the type D module CFD(V) for the surgery framing and the type A module CFA(U) for the standard framing, then form the box tensor product and take homology.
The algebra A(T²) for the torus has two idempotents ι₀, ι₁ and two Reeb chords ρ₁, ρ₂ with differential ∂ρ₁ = ι₀ + ι₁, ∂ρ₂ = 0. The type D module for V with framing p/q is generated by a single generator x with δ¹(x) = (ρ₁)p·x (using the continued‑fraction expansion of p/q to write the monomial). The type A module for U is generated by y with m₂(y, ρ₁) = y and m₂(y, ρ₂) = 0. The box tensor product has generator x ⊗ y; the differential is induced by δ¹(x) ⊗ y + x ⊗ m₂(y,·). Because (ρ₁)p acts as zero on y for p > 0, the differential vanishes and the homology is a free ℤ‑module of rank p, generated by the p distinct idempotent summands. This matches the known result HF̂(L(p,q)) ≅ ℤp.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the rank of HF̂ of a rational homology sphere, first check whether the manifold is an L‑space (e.g. lens spaces, double covers of alternating knots). If it is, the rank equals |H₁|. For non‑L‑spaces, use the surgery exact triangle or the mapping‑cone formula to relate the unknown manifold to a known one. Memorise the bordered algebra for the torus (two idempotents, two Reeb chords) because it appears in every Dehn‑surgery computation.

The Surgery Exact Triangle and the Mapping Cone Formula for Integer Surgeries

For a knot K ⊂ Y and an integer n, the surgery exact triangle relates the hat Floer homologies of Y, Yₙ(K), and Yₙ₊₁(K). The maps in the triangle are induced by cobordisms given by 2‑handle attachments; on the chain level they are represented by counting holomorphic triangles in the symmetric product of a Heegaard surface. Ozsváth and Szabó proved that for sufficiently large n the map HF̂(Y) → HF̂(Yₙ(K)) is an isomorphism, which yields a mapping‑cone formula for the chain complex CF̂(Yₙ(K)). The mapping cone is built from the knot Floer complex CFK̂(K) equipped with the two filtrations (Alexander and Maslov). Concretely, one forms a direct sum of copies of CFK̂(K) shifted by the surgery coefficient, with differential given by the original knot differential plus a “surgery differential” that counts holomorphic disks crossing the basepoint z exactly once. The resulting complex is quasi‑isomorphic to CF̂(Yₙ(K)). This formula makes it possible to compute HF̂ of any integer surgery on a knot in S³ from the knot Floer complex, which is often much smaller than a full Heegaard diagram for the surgered manifold. The mapping‑cone construction also underlies the proof that the correction terms d(Y,𝔰) for large surgeries are given by the formula d(Yₙ(K),𝔰) = d(Y,𝔰₀) − 2Vₖ where Vₖ are the integers defined from the knot Floer homology.

Heegaard Floer Homology of Mapping Tori and the Monodromy Action

Let φ : Σ → Σ be a diffeomorphism of a closed surface of genus g. The mapping torus Yφ = Σ × [0,1] / (x,1) ∼ (φ(x),0) is a 3‑manifold that fibers over S¹ with fiber Σ. Ozsváth and Szabó showed that the Heegaard Floer homology of Yφ can be computed from the induced map φ* on the Floer homology of the symmetric product Symg(Σ). More precisely, there is a spectral sequence whose E²‑page is the homology of the mapping cone of (φ* − id) acting on HF̂(Σ × S¹) and which converges to HF̂(Yφ). When φ is a product of Dehn twists, the action on the Heegaard diagram can be made explicit: each Dehn twist corresponds to a handle slide of β‑curves, and the induced map on the chain complex is given by counting holomorphic triangles with one vertex at the intersection point representing the twist. This description yields a practical algorithm for computing HF̂ of any surface bundle over the circle, provided one can write the monodromy as a word in Dehn twists. A striking application is the proof that if φ is pseudo‑Anosov then Yφ is not an L‑space; indeed, the rank of HF̂(Yφ) grows exponentially with the word length of φ, whereas L‑spaces have minimal rank. The monodromy action also controls the Thurston norm of the fiber class: the Ozsváth–Szabó inequality ‖[Σ]‖T ≤ 2g − 2 + rank HF̂(Yφ) follows from the spectral sequence.

Heegaard Floer Homology and the Thurston Norm: The Ozsváth–Szabó Inequality

For a closed, oriented 3‑manifold Y and a class ξ ∈ H²(Y;ℤ), the Thurston norm ‖ξ‖T measures the minimal complexity of a surface representing the Poincaré dual of ξ. Ozsváth and Szabó proved that if HF̂(Y,𝔰) ≠ 0 for a Spinc structure 𝔰 with c₁(𝔰) = ξ, then ‖ξ‖T ≤ 2g(Σ) − 2 + rank HF̂(Y,𝔰), where Σ is a Heegaard surface used in the definition of the invariant. In particular, for a knot complement the inequality becomes ‖[Σ]‖T ≤ 2g(K) − 2 + rank HFK̂(K), and since rank HFK̂(K) = 2g(K) − 1 for fibered knots, the bound is sharp. The proof uses the adjunction inequality for holomorphic curves in the symmetric product: a holomorphic disk contributing to the differential has boundary on the α‑ and β‑tori, and its domain gives a 2‑chain whose boundary is a linear combination of the curves. The Euler characteristic of this domain yields the genus bound. The inequality has several important corollaries: it detects fibered knots (a knot is fibered iff its knot Floer homology has rank 1 in the top Alexander grading), it gives a lower bound on the genus of a knot in a homology sphere, and it implies that if Y is an L‑space then every non‑zero class in H²(Y) has Thurston norm zero, i.e. Y does not admit a co‑orientable taut foliation. This last statement is one direction of the L‑space conjecture.

  • Confusing the spectral sequence from Khovanov homology with the one from the contact invariant; they converge to different flavors of Heegaard Floer homology.
  • Assuming the bordered pairing theorem works for any decomposition without checking that the boundary parametrizations match the pointed matched circle.
  • Applying the mapping‑cone formula for integer surgeries to rational surgeries without using the rational‑surgery formula of Ozsváth–Szabó.
  • Forgetting that the monodromy action on HF̂(Σ × S¹) is only defined up to homotopy; different factorizations of φ can give chain‑homotopic but not identical maps.
  • Misstating the Ozsváth–Szabó inequality by omitting the rank term; the inequality is an upper bound, not an equality, for non‑fibered classes.
  • Treating the correction term formula d(Yₙ(K)) = d(Y) − 2Vₖ as valid for all n; it holds only for sufficiently large n (n ≥ 2g(K) − 1).
  • Study these points carefully to avoid common mistakes.

hand/siegel-modular-forms.html:
The Fourier–Jacobi Expansion and Jacobi Forms

For a Siegel modular form F of degree g ≥ 2 and weight k, the Fourier expansion with respect to the last diagonal entry of the period matrix Z = ( τ z ; zt τ' ) yields the Fourier–Jacobi expansion

F(Z) = Σm≥0 φm(τ, z) e2πi m τ'

where each coefficient φm is a Jacobi form of weight k and index m on the Jacobi group ΓJ = SL2(ℤ) ⋉ ℤ2. The theory of Jacobi forms, developed by Eichler and Zagier (1985), provides a bridge between Siegel modular forms of genus 2 and classical elliptic modular forms. The Fourier coefficients of φm are indexed by pairs (n, r) ∈ ℤ × ℤ with discriminant Δ = 4nm − r2 ≥ 0, and the transformation law under the Heisenberg part of ΓJ forces the coefficients to depend only on Δ and the congruence class of r modulo 2m. This structure is crucial for the proof of the Saito–Kurokawa lift: the lifted Siegel cusp form has a Fourier–Jacobi expansion whose first non‑zero coefficient φ1 is the classical Jacobi form attached to the elliptic eigenform f via the Shimura correspondence. Moreover, the Maass space can be characterized as the subspace of Siegel modular forms whose Fourier–Jacobi coefficients φm vanish for all m > 1, a fact first observed by Maass (1979) and later refined by Arakawa (1996). The Fourier–Jacobi expansion also underlies the construction of the Ikeda lift, where the higher‑degree Siegel form is built from a compatible family of Jacobi forms of increasing index.

The Koecher Principle and Holomorphy at Infinity

The Koecher principle states that any Siegel modular form of genus g ≥ 2 which is holomorphic on the Siegel upper half‑space 𝔥g automatically extends holomorphically to the Satake compactification; in other words, there are no “cusp singularities” for higher genus. Concretely, if F ∈ Mk(Sp(2g, ℤ)) has a Fourier expansion F(Z) = ΣT≥0 a(T) e2πi tr(TZ) with T running over semi‑positive definite half‑integral matrices, the condition that F be bounded on a Siegel set forces a(T) = 0 unless T is positive semi‑definite. For genus 1 this is false: the classical Eisenstein series E2 has a non‑zero constant term but fails to be modular of weight 2. The Koecher principle is proved by estimating the growth of F on the standard Siegel set 𝔖 = { Z = X + iY : Y ≥ Y0 > 0, |X| ≤ ½ } and using the fact that the symplectic group acts transitively on 𝔥g. A key corollary is that the space of Siegel cusp forms Sk(Sp(2g, ℤ)) coincides with the subspace of forms whose Fourier coefficients a(T) vanish for all singular T (det T = 0). This vanishing property is used in the definition of the Maass lift and in the proof that the Saito–Kurokawa lift lands in the cuspidal subspace. The principle also implies that the Siegel Eisenstein series Ek(g) converges absolutely for k > g + 1 and defines a holomorphic modular form; its Fourier coefficients are given by representation numbers of quadratic forms, a result of Siegel (1935) that links analytic properties to arithmetic of quadratic forms.

Worked Example: Fourier–Jacobi Coefficient of a Saito–Kurokawa Lift
Let f(τ) = Σ a(n) qn be the normalized Hecke eigenform of weight 10 for SL2(ℤ) (the unique cusp form Δ·E4). Compute the Fourier–Jacobi coefficient φ1(τ, z) of the Saito–Kurokawa lift F = Lift(f) of weight 6 for Sp(4, ℤ).
The Saito–Kurokawa lift has Fourier expansion F(Z) = ΣT≥0 A(T) e2πi tr(TZ) with A(T) = Σd|gcd(a,b,c) dk-1 a( (4ac−b2)/(4d2) ) for T = ((a, b/2), (b/2, c)). The Fourier–Jacobi coefficient φ1 collects all terms with c = 1. Setting c = 1 gives discriminant Δ = 4a·1 − b2 = 4a − b2. For each Δ > 0 with Δ ≡ 0,1 (mod 4) there is a unique pair (a,b) up to the action of SL2(ℤ). The coefficient of e2πi (aτ + bz + τ') in φ1 equals Σd|gcd(a,b,1) d5 a(Δ/(4d2)). Since gcd(a,b,1)=1, the sum reduces to a(Δ/4) when Δ ≡ 0 (mod 4) and 0 otherwise. Thus φ1(τ, z) = ΣΔ>0, Δ≡0(4) a(Δ/4) ζΔ qΔ/4 where ζ = e2πi z, q = e2πi τ. This is precisely the Jacobi form of weight 6 and index 1 attached to f via the Eichler–Zagier correspondence.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the first Fourier–Jacobi coefficient of a Saito–Kurokawa lift, remember that only the index‑1 part survives and it is the Jacobi lift of the original elliptic eigenform. Write down the discriminant condition Δ = 4ac − b2 and use the fact that gcd(a,b,c)=1 for primitive T. This reduces the double sum to a single sum over Δ, a standard shortcut that saves time.

The Satake Parameters and the Spinor L‑Function

For a Siegel Hecke eigenform F of genus 2 and weight k, the local Hecke algebra at an unramified prime p is generated by the double cosets T(p) and T1(p2). The eigenvalues λp and μp satisfy the characteristic polynomial

Qp(X) = (1 − αp X)(1 − βp X)(1 − γp X)(1 − δp X)

with αpδp = βpγp = pk−3. The four Satake parameters (αp, βp, γp, δp) are determined up to the Weyl group of type C2. The spinor L‑function is defined by the Euler product

ZF(s) = ∏p (1 − αp p−s)−1 (1 − βp p−s)−1 (1 − γp p−s)−1 (1 − δp p−s)−1.

Andrianov (1974) proved that ZF(s) admits analytic continuation to ℂ and satisfies a functional equation relating s to 2k − 3 − s. For a Saito–Kurokawa lift F = Lift(f) with f of weight 2k−2, the Satake parameters factor as {αp, βp, pk−1, pk−2} where αp, βp are the Satake parameters of f. Consequently ZF(s) = L(f, s) ζ(s−k+1) ζ(s−k+2), matching the product of the elliptic L‑function and two shifted Riemann zeta factors. The standard L‑function L(F, s, St) is the degree‑5 L‑function attached to the standard representation of GSp(4); for a generic (non‑CAP) eigenform it is expected to be entire and satisfy a functional equation of the form s 1−s. The Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture for genus 2 predicts |αp| = |βp| = |γp| = |δp| = p(k−3)/2; this is known for Saito–Kurokawa lifts (where two parameters are powers of p) and for certain Yoshida lifts, but remains open in general. Numerical verification of the Satake parameters via the Hecke eigenvalues computed from Fourier coefficients is a standard computational exercise in the theory of Siegel modular forms.

The Theta Correspondence and the Weil Representation

The theta correspondence, also known as Howe duality, provides a powerful method to lift automorphic forms between members of a reductive dual pair inside a symplectic group. For the dual pair (Sp(2g), O(m)) inside Sp(2gm), the Weil representation ωψ of the metaplectic double cover Mp(2gm) decomposes as a direct integral of tensor products π ⊗ σ where π is an irreducible representation of Sp(2g) and σ of O(m). When m = 1, O(1) ≅ {±1} and the theta lift from Sp(2g) to the metaplectic group Mp(2) recovers the classical Shimura correspondence: a Siegel modular form of half‑integral weight k+½ on the metaplectic group corresponds to an integral weight Siegel modular form on Sp(2g). For m = 2, the dual pair (Sp(4), O(2)) yields the Saito–Kurokawa lift: the theta lift of a holomorphic elliptic cusp form of weight 2k−2 (viewed as an automorphic form on the split torus O(2) ≅ GL1 ⋊ ℤ/2) produces a Siegel cusp form of weight k on Sp(4). The Siegel–Weil formula, proved by Weil (1965) and extended by Kudla–Rallis (1988), identifies the Siegel Eisenstein series Ek(g) with the theta integral of the Siegel theta series attached to the standard lattice ℤ2g. This identity is the analytic engine behind the functional equation of Ek(g) and underlies the proof that the Fourier coefficients of Eisenstein series are representation numbers of quadratic forms. In higher genus, the Kudla program predicts that the Fourier coefficients of the derivative of the Siegel Eisenstein series at its central point encode arithmetic intersection numbers of special cycles on Shimura varieties of orthogonal type. The theta correspondence also explains the existence of the Yoshida lift, which attaches to a pair of elliptic eigenforms (f, g) of weights (k1, k2) a Siegel cusp form of genus 2 whose spinor L‑function is the product L(f, s) L(g, s). This lift is realized by the theta lift from the dual pair (Sp(4), O(2,2)) where O(2,2) ≅ (GL2 × GL2)/GL1.

The Paramodular Conjecture and Abelian Surfaces

The paramodular conjecture, formulated by Brumer and Kramer (2014), predicts a precise correspondence between isogeny classes of abelian surfaces A/ℚ with End(A) = ℤ and paramodular Siegel cusp forms of degree 2, weight 2, and level N equal to the conductor of A. A paramodular form is a Siegel modular form for the paramodular group K(N) ⊂ Sp(4, ℚ), which is the stabilizer of a certain lattice chain; it is the natural level structure for abelian surfaces with non‑split multiplicative reduction. The conjecture asserts that the spinor L‑function ZF(s) of the paramodular form F coincides with the Hasse–Weil L‑function L(A, s) of the abelian surface, and that the Fourier coefficients a(T) of F encode the local point counts #A(𝔽p) via the Eichler–Shimura relation for genus 2. Evidence includes the verification for all abelian surfaces of conductor up to 1000 (Poor–Yuen, 2015) and the proof of the conjecture for abelian surfaces with real multiplication by a quadratic field (Johnson–Leung–Roberts, 2019). The paramodular conjecture is the genus‑2 analogue of the modularity theorem for elliptic curves; its full proof would establish the Langlands correspondence for GSp(4) over ℚ for the discrete series representations of weight 2. Recent work by Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni (2021) on potential automorphy for symmetric powers of Galois representations provides a framework that may eventually yield a proof for a density‑one set of abelian surfaces. Computationally, the space of paramodular forms of level N can be accessed via the Hecke action on the Brandt module of quaternionic orders, and the Fourier coefficients are computed using the Siegel–Eichler mass formula.

  • Confusing the Koecher principle (holomorphy at infinity for genus ≥ 2) with the valence formula for genus 1; the latter does not hold for Siegel modular forms.
  • Assuming the Saito–Kurokawa lift produces all Siegel cusp forms of genus 2; its image is exactly the Maass subspace, a proper subspace when k > 2.
  • Misidentifying the spinor L‑function with the standard L‑function; the spinor L‑function is degree 4, the standard L‑function is degree 5.
  • Thinking the theta correspondence always yields holomorphic forms; the Weil representation can produce non‑holomorphic (Maass) forms unless the dual pair is in the stable range.
  • Believing the paramodular conjecture is proved for all abelian surfaces; it is verified only for conductors up to a few thousand and for special families.
  • Overlooking the role of the Satake parameters in the functional equation of the spinor L‑function; the functional equation relates s to 2k−3−s, not to k−s.
  • Confusing the Fourier–Jacobi expansion with the ordinary Fourier expansion; the former expands in the variable τ' and yields Jacobi forms, not elliptic modular forms.

These advanced topics illustrate how the analytic, arithmetic, and representation‑theoretic facets of Siegel modular forms intertwine, providing a rich source of problems for competitive examinations.
